I farm in Quzhou County on the North China Plain, so at the start of the growing season I would stay with the wheat-maize rotation. That is the system I would trust most at my age because I know the field work, the machinery needs are familiar, and the market is steady enough. Since it is the start of the season, my winter wheat is already in the ground from last autumn, so I would finish that crop well and then follow with summer maize. I would not spread myself across many crops, because that raises labor and management pressure. I would keep most land in the main grain rotation and only leave a small share flexible if needed, but for this year I would still mainly plant grain.

For management, I would keep inputs moderate and practical. On wheat, I would give enough nitrogen to support tillering and grain filling, with phosphorus and potassium as base fertilizer, and I would irrigate at the key stages because spring moisture can be unreliable here. I would use improved seed rather than old saved seed because I want more stable emergence and yield without taking on the cost or risk of something unfamiliar. I would use rotary tillage because it fits common local practice and is easier for me to manage than deeper ploughing every season. I would spray only as needed for common diseases, weeds, and insects, usually a few times rather than too many. After wheat harvest, I would move quickly into summer maize, use hybrid seed, fertilize enough for a solid yield, irrigate a couple of times if rainfall is short, and control weeds and insects with a limited number of sprays. My aim would be a steady harvest with manageable labor, not the highest possible output.
